clue.text: Philosopher’s wedding preparation initially cancelled

indicators.note: the opening letter is the one struck out, as 'initially' points at the start and 'cancelled' means removed

blocks.note: a bride's collection of clothes and linen gathered before the wedding

explanation.surface: A thinker's marriage plans were called off at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay: TROUSSEAU loses its T to give ROUSSEAU.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was the Genevan Enlightenment thinker who wrote The Social Contract.

clue.text: Member of famous quartet proclaimed as celebrity

indicators.note: something proclaimed is announced out loud, so the sound of the name matters here

blocks.note: Ringo, the Beatles' drummer, whose surname has a double R

explanation.surface: One of the Fab Four is hailed as a big name.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous performer or public figure is commonly called this, as in a film or pop idol.

clue.text: Narrow escape from destruction of quakes

indicators.note: destroying something breaks it apart, so these letters are wrecked and rebuilt in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone narrowly survived earthquakes that flattened everything.
explanation.definitionFit: A 'narrow squeak' is an idiom for a close call, a lucky escape by a tiny margin.

clue.text: From bunch of letters in squares, ponder answer

indicators.note: the solution is a run of consecutive letters taken from inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the end of squares joined to the start of ponder

explanation.surface: A crossword solver muses over the letters in a grid before writing in the solution.
explanation.definitionFit: To reply or react to a question is to give a reply, so the verb sense matches.

clue.text: Female garment, for instance, both down and up in new fiction

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means read from bottom to top, so the abbreviation appears once forwards and once backwards
these pieces are placed inside the letters for the new fiction

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example', read downwards
the same abbreviation again, this time to be read upwards
a falsehood or made-up story

explanation.surface: A writer describes a lady's garment in a new novel.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'down' means as written and 'up' means reversed, so the one abbreviation is used twice, once each way, both tucked inside N plus LIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's light, flimsy dressing gown or nightdress, typically of sheer fabric.

clue.text: Script with typo? Calm performance barely finished

indicators.note: a typo is a single mistyped letter, so one letter of the word is swapped for another

blocks.note: the C in this word is mistyped as a T
to calm or soothe

explanation.surface: An editor spots a misprint in a screenplay and stays cool about a show that only just ended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' is the pun: the act ends with the performer bare, not with time running short.
explanation.definitionFit: A burlesque act in which the dancer gradually removes clothing finishes with the performer nearly naked.

clue.text: Part of Labrador first named in indigenous language

indicators.note: this word tells you which piece goes at the front of the joined result

blocks.note: a Labrador is a dog, and a dog's foot is part of it
née introduces a woman's birth name, meaning 'born' or 'named'

explanation.surface: Part of the Labrador region of Canada was first given a name in a native tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: Labrador looks like the Canadian region, but it is the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue spoken by a Native American people of the Great Plains, now living in Oklahoma, shares their name.

clue.text: Cut flowers arranged around it over in shop

indicators.note: cutting trims off the tail end of the word for flowers
turned over, the short word is read from right to left
the shortened flowers go round the outside of the little word

blocks.note: a bunch of flowers arranged together
taken as written

explanation.surface: In a florist's, cut stems are arranged in a display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut flowers' looks like one phrase; Cut is the instruction and flowers arranged is the bunch that loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A small, fashionable store selling clothes or accessories is called by this French-derived name.

clue.text: Almost mate, having backed capture

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
backed means moved backwards, so what is left is read from the end

blocks.note: a mate is a companion or spouse

explanation.surface: A chess player nearly delivers mate after supporting a capture.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess picture misleads: mate is a companion, not checkmate.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch or trap someone, often by deceit, is to ensnare them.

clue.text: Man on board eclipsing second most powerful Russian once

indicators.note: eclipsing means covering or blocking out, so one piece sits around the other

blocks.note: a tar is a sailor, a man aboard ship
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A chess piece outshines the second most powerful Russian of old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man on board' suggests a chessman; it is a sailor on a ship. The definition starts at 'most', not 'second'.
explanation.definitionFit: Before 1917 the emperor ruling Russia held absolute power as its autocratic monarch.

clue.text: Penalties for pupils getting one plus six wrong

indicators.note: wrong signals the letters are in the wrong order and need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Schoolchildren are punished for getting simple arithmetic wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Being thrown out of school is a severe disciplinary sanction for misbehaving students.

clue.text: Decorate sides of bridge and what it overlooks

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

blocks.note: first and last letters of bridge
a ship's bridge looks down on the deck

explanation.surface: Someone adorns the parapets of a bridge and the view below.
explanation.walkthrough: The bridge here is a ship's command post, which stands above the deck.
explanation.definitionFit: To adorn or festoon something with ornaments is to deck it out.

clue.text: Jumble in the box I twice show

indicators.note: a jumble is a muddled mixture, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written, with I used twice

explanation.surface: A jumble sale item twice turns up on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I twice' supplies two I's to the letter pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A public display of art or goods, as in a gallery, is a showing to visitors.

clue.text: Close bonds providing coverage for retirement

blocks.note: near at hand
connections or links

explanation.surface: Strong personal ties ensure financial security in old age.
explanation.walkthrough: Retirement looks like leaving work, but here it is going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightdresses are clothes people wear when they go to bed, so they cover the sleeper.

clue.text: Noble and outstanding saints protecting church

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: owed and not yet paid
S is the abbreviation for saint, doubled for the plural
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A worthy aristocrat and remarkable holy figures shelter a place of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise; here it means still unpaid.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman holding the highest rank of peerage below royalty, or a duke's wife, is an aristocrat.

clue.text: It’ll transform us into superpower – some work essential

blocks.note: a stint of work, as in a night shift
crucial or vital

explanation.surface: A slogan promises that a little effort will make us a world power.
explanation.walkthrough: Held down while typing, it turns lowercase 'us' into 'US', the superpower.
explanation.definitionFit: On a keyboard this button makes letters capitals, so the pronoun becomes the abbreviation for America.

clue.text: Expert in fix put at risk

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the word for fix

blocks.note: to repair
an ace is a highly skilled person

explanation.surface: A specialist caught in a tight spot was in danger.
explanation.walkthrough: Fix reads as a predicament but is the verb meaning repair.
explanation.definitionFit: To be threatened or endangered by something is to be placed in jeopardy.

clue.text: Honoured in retirement Aussie sprinters, holding flag up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word for flag is read bottom to top
holding means gripping on either side, so the birds go round the other piece

blocks.note: emus are fast-running flightless Australian birds
to flag is to grow weary

explanation.surface: Retired Australian athletes are honoured carrying their national flag aloft.
explanation.walkthrough: Sprinters are not athletes but birds; flag is the verb meaning weaken, not a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: A professor who has stepped down keeps the title as an honorary distinction, e.g. professor emeritus.

clue.text: Demolish or rebuild the 2 or 10

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the same materials back together differently, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the answer to 2 down, or equally the answer to 10 across, which has the same four letters

explanation.surface: A choice: knock down or reconstruct buildings numbered two or ten.
explanation.walkthrough: Either cross-reference works, as both answers use the same letters, so the setter offers both.
explanation.definitionFit: To smash something into pieces is to destroy it utterly, wrecking it completely.

clue.text: Express sorrow about large error so unlike good worker

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the sorrowful word goes round the abbreviation

blocks.note: to weep
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels
British slang for a mistake or blunder

explanation.surface: A manager regrets a big mistake that shows the employee is not up to scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: Bish is informal British slang for a mistake, rarely seen outside the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: A diligent employee is tidy and hardworking; a lazy, untidy slob behaves in the opposite way.

clue.text: Extra material tailors put inside vessels

blocks.note: first meaning: linings sewn inside garments
second meaning: large passenger ships

explanation.surface: Tailors stitch extra cloth inside containers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both inner layers of fabric in clothing and big ocean-going passenger ships.

clue.text: Can eye present case, any part of which can be this

definitions.text: Can eye present case, any part of which can be this

blocks.note: surface reading: someone is able to look at a legal case being put forward

blocks.clueFragment: any part of which can be this
blocks.note: setter's reading: can, eye, present and case are four separate nouns, and each can have the same thing done to it

explanation.surface: A lawyer wonders whether they can view the case being presented.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first four words as a list: a can, an eye, a present and a case can each be opened.
explanation.definitionFit: Tins, eyelids, gifts and suitcases are all things one unseals or unwraps, so each may be described this way.

clue.text: Decree from old king or queen followed by uproar about article

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the noise surrounds the little word

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
R stands for Rex or Regina, Latin for king and queen
a loud racket
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A monarch's old edict is greeted by a public outcry over a newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: R works for either monarch, as Rex and Regina share the initial.
explanation.definitionFit: To order or decree officially, as by law or divine authority, is to rule that something shall be.

clue.text: Began after I confused student about it

indicators.note: a confused word is muddled, so its letters are mixed up
about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters wrap round the little word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teacher started things after a muddled pupil got the wrong end of the stick.
explanation.definitionFit: To set up or establish something, such as a rule or inquiry, is to launch or start it.

clue.text: Contemptuously react – gratuitous advice sent back?

indicators.note: sending something back returns it the way it came, so the word runs right to left

blocks.note: tips are both gratuities and helpful hints

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at unsolicited advice and returns it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gratuitous' plays on gratuities, so the word means both money for service and advice.
explanation.definitionFit: Expelling saliva at someone, or saying something venomously, shows scorn or disgust.

clue.text: Little good to be found in evil omen

indicators.note: the small piece is located inside the larger word

blocks.note: wrongdoing
G is the short form of good

explanation.surface: Not much good comes from a sinister portent.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent or indication of what is to come counts as a harbinger of the future.

clue.text: Tolerate European poet, quintessentially English

blocks.note: to brook is to put up with, usually in the negative
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: We can bear a continental poet who seems very English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quintessentially English' is part of the definition, not an instruction to pick letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert Brooke, the First World War poet of 'The Soldier', is famed for his idealised vision of England.

clue.text: Eastern family with disease barely surviving

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for eastern
relatives
a painful joint disorder

explanation.surface: An Asian family struggling with illness are only just getting by.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a scarce supply last, scraping a living with very little, describes subsistence.
